name: Lakota
catalog_quote: The accent is not firmly attached to any particular syllable, but has a definite relation to the position of the syllable. In by far the greatest number of derivative forms the accent is on the second syllable; ... A large number of stems are of the form vc, cvc or ccvc ... In finite form these stems end in a and by far the greatest number have the accent on the stem syllable.
sweep_summary: Both sweep items are the same work: Mirzayan 2010 (Glottolog 158234) and its 2011 citation variant (635449), the CU Boulder dissertation Lakota Intonation and Prosody. scholar.colorado.edu returns 403 to this host), PDF 268 pp. with text layer taken from Wayback capture 20181101031718, saved with extracted text output, and under The work is mainly an AM intonation study, but §3.2.1 (pp. 61-63) states the word-stress facts: second-syllable stress 'for the most part' (Boas & Deloria 1941; Chambers 1978; Shaw 1980/1985 Dakota Stress Rule), many first-syllable-stressed disyllables, most rule-derived but 'synchronically genuine exceptions' remain so stress is written orthographically; §4.2.1 p. 149 'partly predictable... generally appears on the second syllable'; §3.2.2 acoustic study confirms a lexical-stress language. Against the catalog's fixed-strict coding this contradicts strictness while confirming the dominant second-syllable pattern (consistent with the earlier audit's recode-to-fixed-dominant recommendation). It does not supersede Boas & Deloria 1941 as the primary description (its placement passage is a literature summary), and the better modern primary (Ullrich 2008 New Lakota Dictionary / Ullrich & Black Bear 2016 grammar) remains unheld.colorado.edu were rate-limited or blocked; Glottolog, Crossref, marginalia-search, iportal.usask.ca and the Wayback CDX/raw fetch worked. No other stress-titled works exist for lako1247 in the target list.

new_statements.quote: Boas & Deloria (1941) claim that stress placement in Lakota is rule governed. For the most part the stressed vowel is the second one in the word, and generally this is also the second syllable in the word. [...] Chambers (1978) and Shaw (1980) formalize the second syllable stress assignment with a phonological rule. As exemplified even in the earlier periods of the work on Lakota grammar, however, there are many exceptions to the simple pattern of second syllable stress. [...] Despite all the proposed rules, however, there are synchronically genuine exceptions to the assignment of stress by DSR. For this reason the orthographic transcription of Lakota generally marks the location of stress.
new_statements.citation: Mirzayan, Armik. 2010. Lakota Intonation and Prosody. PhD dissertation, University of Colorado at Boulder (Linguistics Graduate Theses & Dissertations 7), 268 pp.
new_statements.locator: §3.2.1 'Previous Descriptions of Lexical Stress and Tone in Lakota', printed pp. 61-62 (pdf pp. 81-82); corroborated by §4.2.1 p. 149 and §1.6 fn. 9 p. 25
new_statements.reading: Lakota has lexical word stress, dominantly on the second syllable (Shaw's Dakota Stress Rule: right-strong binary foot at the left word edge; prefixation keeps stress on syllable 2), with a real class of first-syllable-stressed words (šúNka, wóte, thípi, líla, t'áǧe); many of these are rule-derived in lexical phonology but some are 'synchronically genuine exceptions', which is why stress is written. This supports a dominant/predominant second-syllable coding and is incompatible with a strict (exceptionless) fixed-second-syllable coding; it agrees with the earlier audit note recommending recode fixed-strict -> fixed-dominant. Mirzayan's own first-hand contribution is the acoustic study in §3.2.2 (p. 70: 'Lakota is a lexical stress language'), not a new placement rule.

sources.note: The dissertation is primarily an autosegmental-metrical study of intonation, and the author states he does not analyse the phonology of lexical stress himself (p. 5: 'Previous studies, such as Shaw (1980), Shaw (1985), and Patterson (1990), have addressed the phonology of lexical stress in this language... I simply assume... my impression of the word-level prominence corresponds to this lexical stress'). But §3.2.1 gives a first-hand summary: stress is 'for the most part' on the second syllable (matȟó 'bear', iyáye, lowáNpi, šá), with 'many exceptions' of first-syllable stress in disyllables…

sources.quote: §3: 'The word is the domain of stress in Lakhota. In Lakhota words the first (or only) stressed vowel has higher pitch and greater loudness than all other vowels in that word. Most of the time the stressed vowel is the second one in the word, but this is not always so. It is therefore necessary to write stress on every word. Compare the following Lakhota words from the same verbal paradigm: iya'ye ‘he set out to go there’ e'yaye ‘they set out as a group to go there’.
